answers.question: Does turning off the fans put out a fire in Moon Base air?
answers.answer: The digest cannot confirm that it does. In station-like air, fans-off worked: BASS-II (Abstract, ICES 2019 paper) reports flames always quenched when the fan was turned off, but its tests were at 22.2% oxygen or less, so nothing at Moon Base levels. The ACME BRE report (page 40) found no-airflow flames self-extinguished in normal air within 40 s, yet at 26.5% oxygen and above they were quasi-steady, and at 34% oxygen and 8.2 psia (inside our Moon Base zone) generally persisted 3 minutes or more. Caveat: one 27% test went out at 45 s, and BRE burns gas to imitate solids. Saffire-IV/V (Section IV) say extinguishment in quiescent conditions cannot be assumed rapid at increased oxygen.

answers.question: What tests exist at 30% oxygen or more and low pressure?
answers.answer: Few tests reach the Moon Base zone (30%+ oxygen, 10.2 psi or less). ACME CFI-G: 20 gas-flame tests at 33.2-39.3% oxygen and 0.51 bar (about 7.3 psi); 17 ignited, median 62 s burn (digest). ACME BRE: test 19070D1 at 34% oxygen, 8.2 psia burned steadily with no airflow (BRE final report, page 18). Saffire-VI: VI-2 and VI-3, about 29-31% oxygen at roughly 54-55 kPa (Urban et al., ICES-2024-365; no page given). FLEX has 17 tests at 30-34% oxygen and 10.3-10.5 psi, only edge-of-zone, just above the limit (Dietrich et al., NASA/TP-2015-216046). Note: BASS-II and ACME Flame Design tested nothing inside the zone. Oxygen values at 'edge' are not strictly inside.

answers.question: Which materials behaved differently in microgravity than on Earth?
answers.answer: Several cards show microgravity differences. BASS-II (Summary Report, page 84): PMMA burned down to about 13.5% oxygen in weak flow, below the 15.4% upward-burning limit on Earth. ACME CLD (overview, page 4): methane and ethylene flames had five to eight times more soot than equivalent Earth flames. SPICE (Dotson thesis, page 1): in microgravity, faster airflow or a smaller burner lengthened smoke-point flames. SAME (final report, page 66): smoke particles were typically 50% larger than on Earth. Saffire-II (PSI-99 table, lines 2-5): silicone did not spread in any microgravity sample. These are gas, fuel and smoke tests mostly at near-normal oxygen, not Moon Base conditions.

answers.question: Can a flame relight after it seems to go out?
answers.answer: Yes, in at least one experiment. The CFI report (Nayagam & Dietrich, Cool Flame Investigation Science Final Report, page 6) saw "multiple reignition cycles": the hot flame went out from radiative heat loss, a cool flame followed, then it relit, repeating until the droplet was consumed. The report says this happened at higher pressures (page 8), and CFI notes it was seen above about 2 atm, so it is not Moon Base evidence. The ACME Flame Design final report (page 26) also says a flame may partially extinguish and then reform before complete extinction. CFI data are not fully analyzed (page 7).

answers.question: How long does smoke take to reach a detector on the ISS?
answers.answer: The digest gives no specific time. The closest evidence is a SAME computer model of the station's US Lab: it found mixing dominates smoke transport, so detection lags are longer than in normal gravity, and detection "can be quite long and strongly dependent on location and the presence of obstructions" (SAME final science report, pages 4 and 66). In some low-smoke cases a detector never alarmed in the 300 s simulated (page 65). Our note, not the source's: the model kept the station's normal ventilation on.
